Yes, in C++11 (and later versions), `std::string myString;` calls the default constructor of `std::string`.

The default constructor for `std::string` creates an empty string with zero length. Specifically:
- The string will be empty
- `myString.empty()` will return `true`
- `myString.length()` and `myString.size()` will return 0

Example:
```cpp
#include <string>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::string myString;  // Default constructor called
    std::cout << myString.length() << std::endl;  // Prints 0
    std::cout << myString.empty() << std::endl;   // Prints 1 (true)
    return 0;
}
```

This behavior is consistent across C++11 and subsequent versions of the C++ standard.
